title: Why Traffic Jams Appear Out of Nowhere
alt_hooks: Nobody crashed. Nobody merged. So why did all this traffic just stop?
This traffic jam has no cause. And it's moving backwards.
Somewhere behind you, a traffic jam is being born, and no one did anything wrong.

segments.text: Nobody crashed. Nobody merged. So why did all this traffic just stop?
Get to the front, and there's nothing there. No accident. No roadwork.
segments.visual_intent: camera flies to the empty front of the jam

segments.text: In a 2008 study, researchers in Japan put 22 cars on a 230-metre circular track,
segments.visual_intent: ring track draws on, 22 cars appear

segments.text: and asked every driver to cruise at about 30 kilometres an hour.
The smooth flow didn't last. When one driver eases off a little,
the driver behind reacts a moment late and brakes a little harder. The next driver brakes harder still.
segments.visual_intent: column of cars, braking bars growing

segments.text: Those tiny delays grow into a stop-and-go wave that travels backwards, against the traffic.
On real highways, waves like this drift backwards at roughly fifteen to twenty kilometres an hour.
Later experiments found a single smoothly driven car could dampen these waves.
segments.visual_intent: two rings: all human vs one smooth car

segments.text: So leave a little extra space. You might be the one who smooths it out.
segments.visual_intent: smooth highway, purple car keeps a gap, end card

conclusion: So leave a little extra space. You might be the one who smooths it out.
why_compelling: Opens on a relatable paradox (a jam with no cause), resolves it with a real, visual experiment, then delivers a second twist (the jam moves backwards) and ends with a practical, empowering takeaway.
